common_name: October Skies Aster (Compact Lavender-Blue Native Aster)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun; October Skies is a compact selection of aromatic aster staying much shorter and more mounded than tall wild asters, and it blooms heavily in fall when few other perennials are still flowering.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. October Skies is a compact cultivar of aromatic aster, native to open prairies and glades of the central and eastern United States, forming a dense, rounded mound of fragrant foliage that becomes smothered in masses of small, lavender-blue, yellow-centered daisy flowers in fall, providing crucial late-season nectar for migrating monarch butterflies and other pollinators. Its shorter, sturdier habit compared to taller native asters makes it useful at the front of a border without staking, and it tolerates poor, dry soil and drought exceptionally well once established. Cut back by about half in late spring to keep the plant compact and encourage even fuller fall bloom.

common_name: Purple Dome Aster (Compact Deep Purple New England Aster)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun; Purple Dome is a compact New England aster selection that stays low and mounded without the floppy growth and staking that taller New England asters usually require.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun. Purple Dome is a compact selection of native New England aster, forming a tidy, dense, dome-shaped mound covered in deep violet-purple daisy flowers with golden centers in fall, without the tall, sprawling growth habit that often requires staking in the wild species. This shorter stature makes it far more practical for a mixed perennial border, and like other New England asters it is an exceptional late-season nectar source for monarch butterflies and other migrating pollinators. It performs best with consistent moisture through summer and can be divided every few years in spring to maintain vigor and control spread.

common_name: Gateway Joe Pye Weed (Large Wine-Red-Stemmed Native Pollinator Perennial)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Gateway is a slightly more compact selection of spotted Joe Pye weed, still large but sturdier and less floppy than the wild species.

directions: Plant in consistently moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Gateway is a popular, slightly more compact selection of spotted Joe Pye weed, producing huge, domed clusters of dusty mauve-pink flowers atop sturdy, wine-red-tinged stems in late summer, a magnet for swallowtails, monarchs, and countless other butterflies and bees. Its large scale makes it an excellent back-of-border native for a pollinator garden, rain garden, or pond edge where soil stays reliably moist, and the dried seed heads provide winter interest and food for songbirds if left standing. It spreads slowly to form a substantial clump over time and can be divided in spring if a larger planting is wanted.

common_name: Little Joe Joe Pye Weed (Compact Native Butterfly Perennial)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Little Joe is a compact Joe Pye weed selection that brings the same pollinator value as full-sized Joe Pye species into a much smaller footprint suited to typical garden borders.

directions: Plant in consistently moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Little Joe brings the excellent late-summer butterfly appeal of Joe Pye weed into a compact plant roughly half the size of the towering wild species, producing dense, rounded clusters of dusty rose-purple flowers that draw swallowtails, monarchs, and bees in large numbers without needing the several feet of space required by taller Joe Pye selections. Its smaller stature fits a typical perennial border or rain garden far more easily than full-sized Joe Pye weed, while still providing an excellent native nectar source late in the season. It tolerates average garden moisture better than some Joe Pye species, though consistently moist soil produces the strongest growth and best bloom.

common_name: Golden Fleece Goldenrod (Compact Groundcover Native Goldenrod)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Golden Fleece is one of the most compact, well-behaved goldenrod cultivars, spreading gently rather than aggressively and staying under a foot tall.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade. Golden Fleece is a low, mounding goldenrod selection that stays compact and well-mannered compared to taller, more aggressively spreading goldenrod species, making it a practical choice for a foreground planting or small-space garden without sacrificing the excellent late-season pollinator value goldenrods are known for. In fall it produces abundant sprays of small, bright golden-yellow flowers over glossy, semi-evergreen foliage, drawing large numbers of native bees, butterflies, and other beneficial insects at a time when few other plants are still blooming. Contrary to popular belief, goldenrod does not cause hay fever, since its pollen is heavy and insect-carried rather than airborne; it is a valuable, non-allergenic native for the fall pollinator garden.
